t: Welcome to Dark Souls III, the third and final installment of the acclaimed trilogy. While better-received than Dark Souls II, this title is also a fairly different experience than the first two games, as it draws gameplay elements from all FOUR of From Software's previous Soulsborne titles to create an amalgamation of their respective combat experiences. Combine that with a trophy list that brings back the dreaded ring-collecting, and you're looking at the most complicated trophy list since the original Dark Souls...but fret not, for the guide is here to make it relatively easy on you. Now, this guide intends to walk old and new players alike through the easiest path to the platinum, which means it'll be setting up a build that trivializes most combat, making use of overpowered weapons, and exploiting USB drive/cloud (with PS+) back-up saves to reduce the pain of getting through each area by as much as possible, which drops the general difficulty from a 6/10 to a 5/10, though the playtime estimate also goes up by 20 hours from the assumption that you're playing offline. You're welcome to ignore the advice and recommendations for all of these if you want a greater challenge, but they're present for players who want to enjoy the game, not the struggle. Additionally, while this guide is for the PS4 port of Dark Souls III, it can absolutely be used for the Xbox and PC versions due to their identical achievement lists; we'll also be going over the two acclaimed, but optional DLC expansions near the endgame as well, but you can skip those if you just own the vanilla game. If you DO own them, though, they're well worth playing through from a narrative and loot standpoint. Finally, the difficulty and time estimates above are specifically for the build and playstyle that this guide describes, as you'll be experiencing combat at its easiest but also doing a LOT of grinding for the Covenant items late in the game - if you want a shorter or more traditional experience, you're free to ignore the stat/equipment advice and seek jolly cooperation from other players for those same items, relying on this guide instead for collectibles and boss strategies. No hard feelings!

Before diving into the gameplay details, let's go over the legend for the terms and trophy-relevant items mentioned throughout this guide, which will keep you on-track for the many missable weapons and spells (these will be tracked numerically as well) and let you keep your inventory well-stocked (with or without PS+ backup saves): Item Type Description Trophied Weapons Your main method of damaging and killing enemies and bosses. These vary widely in attack ranges, damage types, and, of course, damage output; notably, if you don't meet the stat requirements of a given weapon (see Gameplay Mechanics for more information on that), its damage and swing speed will be dramatically reduced to the Item Type Description Trophied point where you may as well not use it at all, so you won't be able to use everything you pick up, buy, or forge as soon as you acquire it.

Shields Your main method of defense against enemy attacks. These come in all shapes and sizes, with small ones providing less damage reduction but being great for parrying and large ones being heavy but generally letting you take little to no damage when used. Some also provide passive benefits, like slight HP regeneration, which essentially lets them act as a fifth ring if worn on your back while two-handing a weapon. No Armor Your main method of raising the damage resistances of the Ashen One - and, of course, making them look stylish in a world gone mad. These come in sets that focus on different aspects of defense: some offer high physical damage reduction (usually at the cost of being very heavy), others narrow down to providing resistance to a specific elemental or type of damage, and still others (found in the very early game) just suck. As with weapons, you need to meet a certain stat requirement to properly wear a lot of armor; failing to do so will actually make the armor decrease some of your defenses when worn. No Pyromancies Fire-based magic spells that focus almost entirely on offense with a select few buffing/healing spells. A common and safe choice for players looking for a balance between magic and melee combat, as the spells come early in the game and don't require any stat investments to be effective (though they scale with both FTH and INT). These are cast exclusively with Pyromancy Flames. There are 27 to collect across the game. Yes Miracles "Holy" magic spells that focus on positive buffs to the Ashen One, but which also have some offensive capabilities. A good choice for players looking to supplement their healing and buffing items. These spells require FTH to be used and are cast with chimes. There are 35 to collect across the game. Yes Sorceries Magic spells that focus mostly on offense, with some that alter enemy perception as well. The main attack pool of any mage build with some frighteningly powerful damage potential. These spells require INT to be used and are cast with staves. There are 34 to collect across the game.

Yes Gestures Motions you can have the Ashen One make by pressing TP , then selecting one of seven presets (can be changed in the menu). Very amusing. There are 26 to collect across the game, but you'll be counting from 8 for a total of 33. Yes Rings A special, lightweight form of equipment that provides unique buffs to different aspects of your character and gameplay, though only four can be equipped at a time. Very important and useful. There are 107 to collect in the base game, with the DLC ones not being tracked for the trophy (though they're still GREAT to collect). Yes Crafting Materials Pieces of earthly materials, most commonly Titanite, that are used to upgrade weapons, shields, and armor. Several different tiers of each, the ones used for the final upgrade levels of equipment of course being rarest. Some Consumables One-time use items that heal your character, buff their weapon, cure status conditions, and so on. Several of these can be bought from merchants, but some can only be found as preset item drops. Use wisely. No Key Items Unique items used for story/sidequest advancement, several of which are bought from merchants. Yes Now, you may be wondering (particularly due to the difficulty rating above): how hard IS Dark Souls III relative to other Soulsborne entries? Well, that's a mixed bag, as it's easier and harder

different reasons. Let's outline why - Dark Souls III is: Easier The combat being more aggressive than that of the other two titles means quite a bit less strategy is needed for PvE - the fan-favorite tactic of two-handing a weapon with a shield on the back is more viable than ever here, and once you get the rhythm down, dealing with most enemies isn't complicated. The durability of equipment is back in the hundreds for just about everything, as in Dark Souls I...but the mechanic of their durability being restored every time you sit at a Bonfire is ALSO carried over from Dark Souls II, so you'll almost never have to deal with equipment breaking or getting dangerously degraded, letting you save quite a bit on restoring equipment with Andre. There's no trophy for gathering all unique weapons. Praise the Sun. While not as many as in Dark Souls II, there are phantoms available to summon for several bosses. Doing so increases the boss's HP and defenses to scale their threat level, but this STILL makes most of those bosses easier by giving them another target to focus on while you attack them from behind, and generally, the phantoms can pull their own weight, too. The guide will advise when it's not worth doing so, but this mechanic makes the first playthrough a lot more bearable. Your HP doesn't decrease from dying, though you can still Hollow (and need to for a certain quest) - instead, you can increase it by 30% until the next time you die with Embers, which replace Humanity and Human Effigies while coming a lot easier than those did. As soon as you set up in Firelink Shrine, you'll have a merchant (the Handmaid) to sell anything and everything in your inventory to, so you won't have to worry about excess weapons and armor cluttering up the stuff you actually want to use (and can turn a nice profit on them).

Homeward Bones and the Coiled Sword Fragment (infinitely-usable version of the former, replacing the Aged Feather from the previous game) give you the option to return directly to the last Bonfire used/lit or Firelink Shrine, letting you save quite a bit of time, and activate quite a bit faster to boot if you need to get out of combat ASAP. Occasionally, killing normal enemies will actually refill an Estus Flask for you, which can be a lifesaver in the longer areas. Meanwhile, killing enemy phantoms will always refill 2 Estus Flasks. Some items, like Pine Resins and arrows, refill in your inventory automatically when you rest at a Bonfire if you have enough in storage. Harder The faster, more aggressive combat is a double-edged sword; though it draws from Bloodborne, it lacks the "Rally"/revenge mechanic from there that lets you restore lost HP within a limited window of time by landing your own attacks, so it's very easy to die quickly here if you let down your guard or misread enemy attacks...and if you're more used to the combat of the first two games and Demon's Souls, it's going to take a lot of adjusting to before you're comfortable with this fighting style. For the first time in the overall Soulsborne series, there are three different endings to achieve, each with its own related trophy, AND you have to take three completely different paths to reach each one instead of making last-minute choices on a normal playthrough - that, and the trophy for collecting all the rings (which also ensure you have to refight most of the bosses at least once), means you have to complete three full playthroughs, no stopping halfway or just reloading a pre-ending save. Oh, and the final ending has the most complicated setup of any ending quest up until now, yaaaaaaaaay! With all that out of the way, let's head into what'll be more important to you moment-to-moment: how the game works!

Dark Souls III is designed as an amalgamation of the four previous Soulsborne titles - Demon's Souls, Dark Souls I, Dark Souls II, and Bloodborne - and that led to some notable gameplay changes, relative to the previous Dark Souls titles specifically, that can make jumping from those to this a little jarring if you haven't played the other two titles. They don't necessarily make the game harder once you get used to it, but let's go over the main two changes here and now: First and most notably, combat is way faster and more aggressive now; a sword-and-shield fighting style still works, to be clear (they didn't render shields hysterically useless like in Bloodborne), but you have to react much quicker to enemy attacks and movements, and several of them can perform entire combos on you that stunlock you for several seconds at a time. As a result, more than in either Dark Souls title prior, two-handing your current weapon, leaving your shield on your back, and relying mainly on rolls to avoid or mitigate damage is the most viable strategy, and so the guide is going to advise that for all three playthroughs. Secondly, this is the first Soulsborne title since Demon's Souls to tie magic to a proper "mana bar" (here called Focus) instead of giving spells a preset number of casts that refresh at Bonfires; this same bar also depletes when you use the new Weapon Arts. This can give you more flexibility in how you use magic in combat, and there are a few ways to easily replenish Focus without using a Bonfire, but the build you'll be setting up won't be using any spells until the very late- or post-game, so that won't be especially relevant for the platinum. With those out of the way, let's dive into the general mechanics of the gameplay. On the off-chance that this is your first Soulsborne or it's just been a while since you played one, the guide is going to cover the basics, as well as the intricacies:

As part of its inherent and intended challenge, the combat of Dark Souls III revolves around patience and timing. You're meant to engage only 1-2 enemies at a time, and unless you're dramatically overleveled, even the initial enemies can kill you in a few attacks if you rush in blindly and start mashing buttons; instead, you should be waiting for openings and evading attacks until you can strike. The first part of the combat "equation" is your stamina: the green bar beneath your HP that is drained, either gradually or in chunks, when you attack, block, run, jump, or roll -a.k.a. do almost anything in combat - and refills when none of those actions are being performed outside of a couple of weapon usages. Keeping an eye on this and using it effectively is the key to surviving each encounter, which leads to a sort of "dance" where you use it up with a few attacks and rolls, then hang back from the enemy and let it regenerate. This can thankfully be increased by leveling up your END stat; more on that below. The second part is the enemy itself: every single one has its own set of attacks, reach, and weaknesses to memorize and exploit. For example, one enemy may be large and powerful, but perform slow attacks with several seconds of windup beforehand or "cooldown" afterward in which you can attack them or evade around them; in the same area, maybe even right afterward, another enemy will be smaller with less HP, but move faster and attack at a greater reach, with a third having a particular weakness to fire but wielding a shield that you'll have to work around, and so on. Cater your playstyle to each enemy as you deal with them (until you become overleveled enough to smash everyone's face in with the same weapon)! The third is your equipment load: everything you keep equipped (even when it's not actively being used), i.e., weapons/shields, armor, and rings, has a weight that's added to your total equip burden, which is a fixed amount of 36.5 + your VIT stat x 1.5 (in diminishing returns after a certain point). Your current equipment load is calculated against your equip burden as a percentage of the latter - when at or below 100.0%, your character will move and fight as normal, but when you're above 100.0%, your movement will be slowed across all venues (walking, running, and rolling), which will be a huge hindrance in battle.

In particular, your equipment load constantly affects your stamina and rolling as well, even if it's below 100.0% of your equip burden; the higher it is above 70%, the slower your stamina regenerates and the less distance your rolls cover, with your roll becoming a "fatroll" where your character lands heavily with a slower recovery time and has reduced invincibility. Because of this and the above, you'll want to keep your total equipment load below 70% at all times: 1 weapon and 1 shield at a time, and not wear any heavy armor until you've sufficiently increased your VIT to accommodate for it. Weapons and spells have their damage scale (i.e., increase) with one/two of four related character stats, which is part of how you maximize the damage you're dealing in combat (other than exploiting weaknesses); the higher the letter grade (E -> D -> C -> B -> A -> S), the greater an increase you see per point in the related stat. Generally, the connection is as follows: Large weapons with strong, but slower attacks scale with Strength (STR). Smaller weapons with faster attacks that require more finesse scale with Dexterity (DEX). Miracles scale with Faith (FTH). Sorceries scale with Intelligence (INT). Pyromancies and dark miracles scale with both FTH and INT. There's a type of NPC ally you can summon in levels (and only while you're Enkindled) via glowing gold summon signs: phantoms, who appear near boss arenas and are specifically meant to help you battle said bosses. Though they offer a useful distraction and are often strong enough to hold their own in combat, their presence also increases the defense of the boss they're brought in to fight, so in some cases, their presence can just make life harder.

The guide will advise when it is and isn't worth calling upon them on a boss-by-boss basis. Additionally, a special type of summon sign will summon you into the world of the NPC instead to help them defeat a certain enemy, with the caveat that you have reduced HP and Estus Flasks. This only pops up three times and for two specific characters as you progress their storylines, so the guide will let you know when they're coming. Spells of all types work off a mana system, as mentioned above, but you can only use a few at a time: your Ashen One starts out with a single attunement slot that you can place spells in (with more coming if you level up the Attunement stat) and each one costs a different amount of Focus, or FP, which can only be refreshed by resting at a Bonfire or using certain items. You also have to meet certain INT and FTH stat requirements to not only use, but buy most of these spells. All weapons and some shields possess a special Weapon Art, usable with L2 and consuming Focus, that lets you perform a flashy and usually wide-ranging attack, heal yourself, create extra protection, and so on. Enemies can use these as well, though (and with no FP limit!), so it'll serve you well to learn to recognize them as you play. Safe areas of the game, where enemies do not spawn (though they can follow you there if you initiate combat and run away), are marked with Bonfires, a staple feature of Soulsbornes that you'll quickly come to adore the sight of. Resting in front of one of these with will restore all your lost HP and equipment durability, then respawn all enemies in the world before giving you the options of fast traveling to other Bonfires, attuning spells whose scrolls you own to your limited slots, and accessing the item box, where you can deposit an infinite number of items that you don't need (e.g., excess armor and weapons).

During and outside of combat, you have a few options to heal yourself: Estus Flasks and some spells, which replenish whenever you rest at a Bonfire (Estus Flasks also have a chance to replenish by 1 after you kill about 10-20 enemies); and certain equipment that gradually heals you. The crucial thing to know is that only the Estus Flasks and spells heal you immediately, though the equipment is absolutely worth using between battles for how it lets you save those for actual combat. You'll also quickly gain access to an Ashen Estus Flask, used to restore your Focus gauge; the game makes you divide additional gained Flasks between these and the regular Estus Flasks, though you can alter the amount you carry of each by simply going to Andre, and because your build doesn't rely on spells or Weapon Arts, you consequently won't need any of these. Every piece of equipment you wear and use also has durability, which is worn down from a fixed maximum value every time you attack with a weapon or take a hit while wearing armor and causes the item to "break" when it reaches 0, severely reducing its effectiveness and forcing you to repair it for Souls at Andre. However, there are three ways to restore durability before the breaking point: 1. The simplest method is an automatic one: every time you rest at Bonfires, all of your equipped items have their durability restored to full, just like your HP. Considering that you'll be doing this quite frequently in the process of clearing out areas, you therefore shouldn't have to worry about durability getting super low unless you're on the receiving end of an attack specifically targeting item durability (which does exist - a couple of enemies can do this, and if you get into PvP other players have access to spells with the same effect). In fact, the durability of equipment has been pumped up so much from Dark Souls II (and durability for rings has been removed altogether) that you'll almost never risk breaking anything as you play. 2. Partway into the game, you'll gain access to the Repair sorcery, which will restore 20 durability to all currently-equipped items and can be used quite a few times even with your starting Focus gauge without Bonfire rests; however, you need 15 INT to cast it. 3. Infrequently throughout the game, you'll come across Repair Powder that offers the same effect as the above; you should only use either if you're far from a Bonfire with enemies to go and one or more suddenly-low durability items equipped.

As in all modern From Software titles, death is a mechanic and valuable teacher; Soulsborne games are designed around the idea that, while a setback, death is meant to teach you what not to do in combat and exploration, leaving you with an idea of how to do better on the next run. When you die, you'll lose your Souls and, if Enkindled, a sizable chunk of your HP bar: reclaiming the latter requires the usage of an Ember, while the latter is left at or near the location of your demise and can be collected by simply walking up to it and pressing ...except if you die before reaching it, at which point they disappear forever. Now, for this walkthrough, you're encouraged to make use of backup saves as often as you'd like (with PS and/or a USB drive) to make life easier - but if you're good enough and/or want to do this 100% legitimately, that's not at all a requirement. Now, let's compile the combat controls, as the tutorials are only located in the starting area of the game. Button Action R1 / L1 Standard attack; for melee weapons, this is a light attack, while for catalysts/chimes, this will cast your currently selected spell. R2 / L2 Special attack; for melee weapons, this is a slow and heavy but stronger attack, while for catalysts/chimes, this is a melee attack to be used when you're out of spells. Switch your weapon to a two-handed grip for increased melee damage; press this a single time to do so for your right-hand weapon, and hold it down to do so for your left-hand weapon. Use your currently selected consumable item. Cycle through your available spells; whatever you leave displayed is what you'll use when you press R1 / L1 with the appropriate weapon (so long as you have enough FP left). Cycle through your consumable held items; whatever you leave displayed is what you'll use when you press (so long as you still have at least 1 left).

Cycle through your equipped right-hand weapons. Cycle through your equipped left-hand weapons. R3 Lock onto the nearest enemy; you can switch between targets with R R . L + (press) Roll in any direction, with speed and landing determined by your equipment load; this provides "I-frames", about 1/2 of a second where your character is immune to damage, so you can either roll away from or through attacks without losing any HP if you time it right. However, this drains your stamina gauge just like attacking, so you can't do it indefinitely. Controls Button Action L + (held) Run instead of walking; this consumes your stamina gauge, so you can't do so indefinitely. R1 while undetected behind enemy Backstab, dealing massive damage and knocking them down; you need to be extremely close to them for this to work properly, otherwise you'll just perform a normal attack. R1 while falling Falling attack, which hits for higher damage and knocks normal-sized enemies down, though it doesn't negate any damage you take from falling unless you land on a large enough enemy. L2 / R2 with shield while being attacked Parry, which deflects your enemy's attack and leaves them briefly off-balance; this leaves them open to a riposte, a.k.a. the frontal equivalent of a backstab, with your R1 / L1 weapon. And finally, let's talk about stats, the most enduringly important part of any RPG. There are two separate lists you'll be keeping track of: Player stats, which determine the attributes of your Ashen One and their ability to wield certain equipment (each has a "soft cap" level at which you begin receiving diminishing returns from putting more levels into it); Equipment stats, which determine the damage output/resistances and longevity of each piece of armor and weaponry.

Attribute Icon Effects Soft Cap(s) Vigor (VGR) Determines HP (initially increases by roughly 30 with every level) 18 (1 less HP with each level) 50 (only +2 HP per level) Attunement (ATN) Determines number of attunement slots (storage space for magic of all types, can only use what's slotted in during battle) Determines Focus (in gradually increasing amounts until 35) 35 (only +2-3 Focus per level) Endurance (END) Determines stamina (initially increases by 2 with every level) Raises lightning resistance and, to a lesser extent, other defenses and all resistances with every level 40 (+1 stamina every 6 levels) Vitality (VIT) Determines equipment load (increases by 1 with every level) Raises physical defense and poison resistance, as well as, to a lesser extent, all other resistances 40 (physical defense and poison resistance increase at a fraction of their former rate) Strength (STR) Increases damage for weapons that scale with strength (e.g., clubs, broadswords) Two-handing with "multiplies" your Strength by 1.5, allowing you to effectively wield weapons that otherwise require a higher stat value Raises fire resistance and, to a lesser extent, all other defenses and resistances with every level 40 (lower amount per level) 60 (multiple levels needed for each increase) Dexterity (DEX) Increases damage for weapons that scale with dexterity (e.g., polearms, daggers) 40 (lower amount per level) 50 (no longer increases Player Stats Attribute Icon Effects Soft Cap(s) Reduces spellcasting time and damage sustained from falling spellcasting speed) 60 (multiple levels needed for each increase) Intelligence (INT) Determines damage for weapons and spells that scale with INT Raises magic defense and, to a lesser extent, all other defenses and resistances with every level 40 (reduced increases across the board) 60 (further reduction in increases across the board)

Faith (FTH) Determines damage for weapons and spells that scale with FTH; slightly more effective at increasing damage for dark miracles and pyromancies than INTis Raises dark defense and, to a lesser extent, all other defenses and resistances with every level 40 (reduced increases across the board) 60 (further reduction in increases across the board) Luck (LCK) Increases Item Discovery (chance of enemies dropping items upon death) by 1 with every level Slightly raises all defenses and resistances with each level, as well as increasing curse resistance at certain levels Increases the damage of Hollow-infused weapons and two other weapons (Man-Grub's Staff, Anri's Straight Sword) None Offensive Attributes Attribute Icon Determines: Weapon Category The type of weapon you're currently wielding, which determines what kind of attacks you can perform with it, its swing speed and range, how much stamina is consumed per attack, and (usually) the Attack Type. Below is a brief list of the different weapon categories and how they handle in combat: Daggers: Rapid attacks for minimal stamina, high-damage Backstabs/Ripostes, and great utility with elemental damage-buffing items, but a short attack range, low damage, and inability to parry heavy weapons. Straight Swords: Medium-damage attacks for medium stamina, great for elemental infusions via upgrades, and one of the best options to use in tandem with shields, making them a solid starting weapon. Greatswords: Long-range and high-damage attacks that can easily hit and stagger multiple enemies at once, but consume a lot of stamina with every swing. Ultra Greatswords: Immense damage and an almost guaranteed stagger with every attack, but equally great stamina consumption and a very high stat threshold (STR and VIT) to clear for proper usage.

Curved Swords: Faster versions of Straight Swords that work best against lightly-armored enemies and replace the kick animation with a dodge that simultaneously damages the enemy. Katanas: Great at inflicting high damage and lots of bleed at any range, as well as allowing for parrying when equipped as your left-hand weapon...but low, low durability, preventing prolonged use without Bonfire rests. Equipment Stats Attribute Icon Determines: Curved Greatswords: Higher damage, but slower swings and a shorter range than regular Greatswords. Piercing Swords: Performs thrust attacks that do great damage against heavily-armored or -scaled enemies and can unleash powerful Ripostes, but are easily evaded due to the small area of their attacks. Axes: Decently quick attacks for medium damage that can hit multiple opponents in a group and dependent solely on STR without DEX, but with a shorter range than most normal-sized swords. Great Axes: Very high-damage attacks that easily break through blocking enemies' shields, but slow, very heavy, short-range, requiring very high STR to wield, and consuming lots of stamina with each swing. Hammers: High-damage attacks that work best against heavily-armored targets, have a high chance to stagger, and become faster if the first attack of a combo hits, but leave you open to retaliation if you miss. Great Hammers: Largest weapons in the game with great range and extremely high damage that's guaranteed to stagger most enemies, but extremely slow and stamina-intensive in use. Fist Weapons: Fast attacks that don't require much stamina and (when using claws) inflict bleed with each strike, but also have the shortest range of all weapons in the game. Spears: Long reach and high damage with potential to "turtle" when used with a shield to attack enemies while defending, but a narrow attack range that's worthless against fast opponents.

Halberds: Long sweeping attacks that work well for crowd-control and deal high damage when striking an enemy at the edge of their range, but otherwise deal half-damage and consume lots of stamina. Reapers: Scythes that can deal high damage and bypass an enemy's shield if you hit them at the exact right angle and range, but otherwise consume lots of stamina and can be easily Parried. Whips: Have an unpredictable attack pattern that hits multiple enemies and can't be Parried or Riposted, but also can't perform special attacks and are weak against armored/scaled enemies...save this for PvP. Bows: Allows you to manually aim ranged projectiles (arrows) that automatically perform a Critical Hit whenever you hit an enemy or boss in the head, but otherwise does low damage and is reliant on ammo. Greatbows: Larger Bows that do more damage per shock and can knock down some enemies, but fire slower and require you to stand in place during the process. Crossbows: Fire faster than Bows and can have their arrows infused with an element for higher damage, but reload slower and can only be manually aimed when two-handed. Flames: Used to cast pyromanciesand are upgraded with Souls, but require a lot of points in INT and FTH to actually use. Chimes/Talismans: Used to cast miracles and require a FTH threshold to be met before you can wield them effectively. Staves: Used to cast sorceries and require an INT threshold to be met before you can wield them effectively. Attack Type The damage type of the weapon in question, which is always 1-2 out of the following three: Strike: blunt and wide, reserved for hammers, gauntlets, and staves. Best results against armored opponents. Slash: thin and fast, reserved for swords, scythes, axes, whips, and daggers. Best results against unarmored or lightly armored opponents.

Thrust: narrow and precise, reserved for lances, halberds, spears, twinblades, greatswords, and arrows. Best results against unarmored or lightly armored opponents. Attribute Icon Determines: Weapon Art The special skill that you can perform with the weapon (or, sometimes, shield) by pressing L2 , which vary in usefulness. Only some are completely unique, with the rest being shared between weapon categories. FP Cost How much Focus using the Weapon Art costs you. Physical ATK How much physical damage attacks deal; for melee weapons, this is the base damage of each attack. Magic ATK How much magical damage attacks and sorceries deal; this exploits weaknesses to magic. Fire ATK How much fire damage attacks and pyromancies deal; this exploits weaknesses to fire. Lightning ATK How much lightning damage attacks and miracles deal; this exploits weaknesses to lightning. Dark ATK How much dark damage attacks and dark miracles deal; this exploits weaknesses to dark. Critical Multiplier How much extra damage backstabs and ripostes performed with a given weapon deal. Bleed Effect How much bleed buildup attacks and spells inflict; when the meter fills, the target bleeds, removing a large chunk of their HP in seconds. Poison Effect How much poison buildup attacks and spells inflict; when the meter fills, the target is poisoned, gradually draining their HP over time. Frost Effect How much frost buildup attacks and spells inflict; when the meter fills, the target is frostbitten, hampering their movements and slowing their stamina regeneration. Shot Range The range that arrows and other projectiles you fire can travel before falling off in both velocity and damage. Spell Buff How much the wielded weapon strengthens spells that you cast with it; note that this doesn't apply to every single spell in the game (e.g., Pestilent Mist deals a fixed percentage of the enemy's HP).

Defensive Attributes Attribute Icon Determines: Physical Absorption How much physical damage from enemy attacks is reduced by your armor or shield (when blocking with it): the higher the number, the more damage is mitigated, which is true for all absorption and reduction stats. It's also based on your original defensive stats, so it's important to keep those high. Magic Absorption How much magical damage from enemy attacks is reduced by your armor or shield. Fire Absorption How much fire damage from enemy attacks is reduced by your armor or shield. Lightning Absorption How much lightning damage from enemy attacks is reduced by your armor or shield. Dark Absorption How much dark damage from enemy attacks is reduced by your armor or shield. Bleed Resistance How much bleed buildup from enemy attacks is reduced by your armor. Attribute Icon Determines: Poison Resistance How much poison buildup from enemy attacks is reduced by your armor. Frost Resistance How much petrify buildup from enemy attacks is reduced by your armor. Curse Resistance How much curse buildup from enemy attacks is reduced by your armor. Poise How much damage you can take mid-attack without being staggered out of it; it's not 1:1, but the higher it is, the harder it will be for enemy attacks to stagger you mid-swing. When not attacking, though, it isn't relevant. Stability How much stamina you lose when blocking enemy attacks; the higher the value, the higher the percentage of stamina preserved after blocking an attack. This can only go up to 85 (a.k.a 85%), but if your build revolves around waiting for openings left by enemy attacks, you want this as high as possible. Durability How many hits a piece of equipment can deal and take before breaking; generally, this value decreases by 1 with every 10ish hits dealt (for weapons) and received (for armor). When it reaches 0, the equipment is broken and useless in combat, and you'll need to repair it via Andre or Repair as Bonfires will no longer restore it.

Weight How much a piece of equipment contributes to your equipment load; balancing this and keeping an eye on the percentage of your equipment burden that you're currently making use of is crucial for determining how effective your rolls and general movement will be. And with all that outlined, let's finish with your character build (that is recommended)!

As in Dark Souls II, magic-based builds have unfortunately been nerfed since this game's release, and while some spells remain useful for certain boss fights, by and large, you'll be much better served by an otherwise-pure melee build. To that end, you'll be starting off as a Knight, which not only does a decent amount of damage with their starting weapon, but is also moderately sturdy, making it an excellent setup for old and new players alike - later on, however, you'll have to switch to the most broken and easiest-to-use weapon in the game, setting up a DEX build in the process (yeah, yeah, filthy scrubs that you are), that'll get you to the platinum with relative ease with this stat array: This isn't the final level you'll reach (particularly if you're playing through the two DLCs and especially if you do your Covenant grinding offline), but this is the baseline you'll reach by the end of the first playthrough. Let's go over why you want this: VGR 45: While it won't always be a priority to increase, having a healthy amount of HP is always important in any RPG, even this one. You'll be scaled accordingly as enemies start getting tougher. ATN 10: This is how much you start with, and you don't need any more - the one slot it gives you is more than enough, as there are a couple rings that can give you more if necessary. END 35: Your survival in a given fight will often be determined by how much stamina you have left to roll or run with. After 40 this becomes almost worthless to dump points into for the sheer diminishing returns you get, but getting here or to the softcap will help keep you alive. VIT 35: This is what will most often be the focus of your level-ups, as maintaining a <70% equipment load to preserve your roll and speed is CRUCIAL to every single battle in the game. Helps that it also shores up your defense against most attacks like nothing else.

STR 13: This one's a bit misrepresentative - you'll actually be putting points into this in the early game as you continue using regular swords, but once you get the Sellsword Twinblades later on, you'll be using the in-game respec option to transfer those points to... DEX 36: Because it determines the damage of the Sellsword Twinblades (and does so by itself once you use a certain infusion on them later), it's the first stat you'll raise to exactly the softcap over the course of the entire playthrough. It'll help tremendously, believe it. INT 9: As with STR above, you'll be putting exactly one point into this to gain (purchasing) access to the majority of the game's sorceries, then relocating it to a more useful stat later on. That said, you're welcome to dump points into it if you want to use sorceries in later playthroughs once you've reached the soft cap on the important ones. FTH 9: It's not advised to touch this at all during the first playthrough because the main miracle vendor is nice enough to talk to you without raising it to 10, but as with INT above, you're welcome to dump points into it if you want to use miracles in later playthroughs once you've reached the soft cap on the important ones. LCK 8: Well, you don't really need to put any points into this until you get to item-grinding near the end of the first playthrough, and even then the equipment you'll have access to will more than supplement the need for dumping into this. So, the first thing you'll be doing is increasing your INT to 10 so you can recruit Orbeck, then you'll cycle through the rest of the stats according to what's most useful for the next section of the game each time. As far as equipment goes - you'll be finding many, many options for weapons and armors throughout the game, and the guide will make note of which ones are worth actually using, so don't worry about having to trial-and-error your way through that.

Then there's how you'll want to play: you COULD still hide behind a shield from all attacks and peek out to stab at enemies until they're dead (this strategy is commonly called "turtling"), but the faster method that fits better with the game's aggressive combat is to two-hand your weapon with to hit for more damage and cut a swathe through enemies, rolling and evading around them as needed - the author got through the entire game without needing to resort to his shield in combat, just by being overpowered damage-wise. And with that, just about everything you need to know has been covered in too much detail! Time to begin your quest into Lothric... DARK SOULS I & II ASPECTS So, a criticism among many players of this game and fans of the overall franchise is how much Dark Souls III pulls from the original Dark Souls vs. its sequel, the much more divisive Dark Souls II. It's entirely up to each individual player whether or not it takes too much from the former or too little from the latter, but if you're at all interested in comparing and contrasting the two, the author tallied up all reappearing elements, characters, and continued storylines from the two games here; the first game is definitely more integral to the overall plot, but the author found the stuff from the second to be implemented pretty fairly. That said, there's no good way to hide these with the spoiler toggle because of how it affects formatting, so if you're going in blind and don't want to read this just yet, go ahead and skip to the first walkthrough section, Cemetery of Ash. Otherwise, enjoy! Dark Souls I: Andre of Astora returns to once again be the player's blacksmith - and the only one in the game this time. Relatedly, the corpse of the Giant Blacksmith is found in Anor Londo, and the ember he carries, as well as Andre when spoken to later, confirms his identity and friendship with the Chosen Undead.

Gwyndolin returns and plays a substantial role in the backstory of the game, not only having become the new leader of the (remaining) gods but having also hidden his younger sister, Yorshka, away from the Cathedral of the Deep and Pontiff Sulyvahn before being consumed by Aldrich, Devourer of Gods. The Lifehunt Scythe returns as a miracle devised by Aldrich seeing Gwyndolin's memories of Crossbreed Priscilla while sleeping, thereby confirming the latter's survival. Good ol' Patches comes back after being absent in Dark Souls II, this time with the moniker of "Unbreakable" but otherwise meant to be the same one from the original game. Havel the Rock's armor, club, shield, and ring are all available to wear and use, with an NPC using them against you in Archdragon Peak. The entire equipment set of Solaire of Astora can be obtained from Pickle-pee Pump-a-rum, with his sword being found in a Mimic. The Silver Knights of Anor Londo and Black Knights that descended into the Kiln of the First Flame with Gwyn return, the former guarding what's left of Anor Londo and the Untended Graves while the latter can be found scattered across the other areas of the game. Anor Londo reappears as the upper section of Irithyll of the Boreal Valley, which is revealed to be the ground-level city visible from the cathedral in the original game. Within, the former chamber of Gwynevere is accessible, though she's long since departed, leaving behind her Sun Princess Ring; the Dancer of the Boreal Valley and Rosaria are implied to be two of her children. The Smouldering Lake connects directly to the Demon Ruins filled with the corpses of Taurus Demons and Asylum Demons, making it what's left of Lost Izalith. Additionally, said ruins contain the corpses of the Fair Lady and what's either her servant, Eingyi, or her sister, Quelana, in what used to be her chamber.

An old and crumbling Asylum Demon, here called the Stray Demon, can be fought atop the wall encircling Farron Keep. The legacy of Artorias lives on in the Abyss Watchers, who emulate his fighting style, serve under what might be Sif, and are dedicated to wiping out the Abyss wherever it crops up. You can also get his weapons through their Covenant and his armor from the Handmaid. Gwyn's exiled son, the Nameless King, finally appears as one of the hardest bosses in the series and has the reason for his erasure from history explained - he allied with the dragons against the gods. Ornstein and Smough both return in different capacities; Ornstein is revealed to have left Anor Londo in search of his master, the Nameless King (you find his armor outside the latter's arena), while Smough stayed behind to defend Gwyndolin and perished against Aldrich. The rings of Gwyn's Four Knights can be found across the game. The masked Giants return, mainly as slaves but with one (possibly a descendant of Gough) set up as an archer in the Undead Settlement. Siegward of Catarina is an oblique reference to and reimagining of Siegmeyer, though more successful in his quest. Flynn's Ring returns and admits the original tale of the hero was a fable. The Crystal Sages have succeeded Big Hat Logan as sorcerers and directly studied his work. The Brigand found outside the Cathedral of the Deep is set up almost exactly like a Brigand Chosen Undead would be. Kirk returns, this time as a member of Rosaria's Fingers with the appellation Longfinger. Kaathe plays a very indirect role in the plot - the implication is that he was behind the Abyss outbreaks that the Abyss Watchers responded to, several statues bearing his likeness appear in Lothric Castle to suggest that he had a hand in creating the kingdom, and one of his, uh, holes (that the Primordial Serpents pop out of to talk to people) is present in the Ringed City, indicating that he communicated with some of its residents. Most importantly, however, Yuria carries on his mission by influencing the Ashen One to bring about an Age of Hollows.

The Bonewheel Skeletons return once again!...and have been nerfed so much that they're barely a threat now. The armor of Black Iron Tarkus reappears on the shoulders of the badass Knight Slayer Tsorig, with the Handmaid selling it to you later. The Man Serpents are present just before the Untended Graves and more prominently in Archdragon Peak, as warped descendants of the originals in Sen's Fortress. The Calamity Ring of Kalemeet can be obtained in Archdragon Peak and now makes fun of players who use it. A Man Serpent Mendicant in Archdragon Peak can summon the Unkindled Prince, indicated to be Prince Ricard from the original game. The Painted World of Ariandel is heavily implied to be the original Painted World of Ariamis, painted over many times in the intervening eons between games, by the presence of Crossbreed Priscilla's arena at the very bottom of the ice chasm. The ruins of the original Firelink Shrine can be found in the base of the massive tree where you battle The Demon Prince. In the second phase of the final boss, the Soul of Cinder, Gwyn wrests control over the incarnation of all Lords of Cinder and shows you what a REAL fight (without ripostes) against him looks as an altered version of his boss music starts playing. Dark Souls II: A deceased Giant grown into a tree can be found just outside the Firelink Shrine. Creighton the Wanderer returns, this time as an invading member of Rosaria's Fingers and foe of Sirris, where he's confirmed to be a serial killer like Pate. The entire equipment set of Lucatiel of Mirrah can be obtained from the Handmaid, the Soul of the Rotted Greatwood, and Pickle-pee Pump-a-rum, with the latter giving you her helm that confirms the Bearer of the Curse ensured her name would be remembered. Knight Slayer Tsorig wields both the Fume Ultra Greatsword and the Ivory Warrior Ring from the Crown of the Old Iron King and Crown of the Ivory King DLCs, implicitly because he killed their original owners.

The Pursuer's Greatshield returns as the Curse Ward Greatshield, now rotated 90 degrees and offering a completely inverted effect. Vendrick's Shield of Want can be found in the Smouldering Lake, its description indicating that he went down in history as a false and greedy king; meanwhile, Nashandra's portrait is found next to Gwynevere's in Anor Londo, suggesting that her reputation remained unmarred despite her true nature as a Child of Dark. The same area also seems to contain a painting of the Throne of Want. The Manikin Claws return, now as weapons used by the Sable Church of Londor. A pair of Drang Knights are fought in Anor Londo and are directly noted to hail from Drangleic, with their dual-wielded weapons referencing the second game being the only one in the trilogy to have an established dual-wielding mechanic. Alva and Zullie have their offscreen relationship brought to a tragic end, with Zullie fleeing him and later dying in the Ringed City while Alva became the Seeker of the Spurned, invading the Ashen One twice in search of her. The body of Laddersmith Gilligan is found in the Profaned Capital, having continued to make ladders until dying/Hollowing or being killed by the people he pissed off in the second game. The Greatshield of Glory, formerly wielded by the Drakekeepers, returns in the Profaned Capital with a mention of the glory it represented. Lion Knight Albert guards the way to Prince Lothric and comes from the fallen land of Forossa, wearing the Faraam Set, the main armor associated with the Bearer of the Curse, which can be bought from the Handmaid late in the game and mentions the game's tagline of "going beyond death". Soul Stream mentions a scholar that doubted the process of Linking the Fire and steered Prince Lothric toward the same mindset - this is either Pontiff Sulyvahn, indicated by a statue of Prince Lothric wielding his Profaned Greatsword, or Aldia, who's both the most famous scholar in the series and the creator of the original version of Soul Stream, as well as the first to provide an alternative to the cycle of Fire and Dark.

The Drakeblood Knights are summoned by a Man Serpent Mendicant in Archdragon Peak, with one of their corpses also providing the gesture needed to even reach the area. Karla explicitly confirms herself to be a Child of Dark like Nashandra, Elana, Nadalia, and Alsanna. The ruins of Earthen Peak are present among the wreckage of the Dreg Heap, with Mytha's poison pools still lingering and several Poison Beetles scattered about while the last of the Desert Pyromancers, Zoey, leads the remaining Thralls. The Ruin Set, detailing the fate of the knights that would inspire the Ruin Sentinels, is found in the Ringed City. LORE Now, like every Soulsborne title, Dark Souls III's story is intentionally fragmented, and while you're given quite a bit of the main plotline via dialogue with the Fire Keeper and other important NPCs, many of the details are relegated to item descriptions and visual hints that you might not find while you're playing. However, if you're interested in knowing the full tale of Lothric, the guide will be laying out the tale as it's presented in timeline order (with references!); there's no good way to hide these with the spoiler toggle because of how it affects formatting, so if you don't want to read this just yet, go ahead and skip to the first walkthrough section, Cemetery of Ash. Otherwise, enjoy!

In the beginning of time, Gwyn discovered the First Flame and, alongside the other bearers of the Lord Souls, fought to dethrone the Everlasting Dragons that ruled the world in order to begin an age of Fire; in this, he was aided by the Pygmies, the primordial humans who wielded weapons and spells forged from Dark.[1] Despite their repeated success in combat, however, Gwyn feared the Pygmies' mastery over their shared Dark Soul and the threat it could represent to his age of Fire enough that he took several drastic actions to limit them: he never celebrated or recorded their victories in the annals of history,[2] he gifted them a Ringed City designed specifically to seal them away from the rest of the world and time itself,[3] and most catastrophically, he placed a seal of Fire upon their weapons and armor to suppress their access to the Dark - this would become the Darksign that would be passed down to all humans, causing them to begin Hollowing whenever the First Flame would weaken in the future and let the Dark within them spiral out of control, which would lead to countless tragedies and fallen kingdoms.[4] During and after this time, Gwyn had five children, all of whom he used to his own ends or mistreated extensively; to begin with, his firstborn and most powerful son (possibly named Faraam)[5] who fought alongside him in the war against the Dragons came to turn on him, siding with the mortal enemies of the gods,[6] which forced Gwyn to strip him of much of his godly power and erase his name from history,[7] leaving the now-Nameless King and his stormdrake, the King of the Storm, to reside in the Archdragon Peak.[8] His second son, Gwyndolin, was born with an affinity with the moon, which Gwyn considered feminine in contrast to his own affinity with the sun, and so Gwyn forced Gwyndolin to present as a woman for centuries, to the latter's great displeasure.[9] His first daughter, Gwynevere, would be the only one to continue the bloodline of their family, giving birth to Rosaria,[10] the one who would become the Dancer of the Boreal Valley, [11] and several others before abandoning Anor Londo altogether alongside many other gods.[12] Meanwhile, Gwyn all but completely ignored his second daughter, Yorshka, who would be raised and named by her brother Gwyndolin instead.[13] Finally, his youngest daughter, Filianore, suffered the most tragic fate of all - she was gifted to the Pygmies alongside the Ringed City as a show of good faith from Gwyn[3] and, though treasured by them, was forced to enter an eternal slumber that kept the city frozen in time[14] and thus hidden from the rest of the world at the bottom of the Dreg Heap.[15] In the eons following Gwyn sacrificing himself to maintain the First Flame,[16] innumerable kingdoms would rise and fall around the world; this would include Forossa[5] and Drangleic.

[17] Many of these were burned down by the Abyss Watchers, also known as the Undead Legion, [18] inheritors of the blood of the wolf and the legacy of Artorias,[19] considered to be the first of their ranks,[20] who bonded with the great wolf through the sharing of their blood[21] and fought a constant shadow war against the Abyss, with the very silhouette of their armor coming to be considered an ill omen by the masses.[22] Their fighting style was an unorthodox homage to that of Artorias,[23][24] emphasizing speed[25] and forgoing any sort of shield, which led to Hawkwood being ostracized despite ironically matching Artorias's own preferences.[26] They also had two other ranks of warriors to aid them - the Farron Followers who honorably killed in combat any members who fell to the Abyss,[27][28] and the Watchdogs of Farron who guarded the Farron Keep where they were laid to rest.[29] Eventually, the Abyss Watchers would descend into the Kiln of the First Flame and Link the Fire as one, refusing to sacrifice any one member over the rest, but when they were resurrected by the tolling of the bell, they were tragically forced to endlessly cut each other down as their ranks kept rising with the Abyss in their hearts.[30] However, several kingdoms would persist in one form or another for eons and even to the last Linking of the Fire, including the shadowy land of Londor, the dreaded and secretive[31] home of Hollows who disguise themselves as intact humans,[32] founded by three sisters[33] under the mentorship of the Primordial Serpent Kaathe[34][35] and seeking to create a Lord of Hollows that will end the age of Fire in favor of the Dark.[34] Another was the sandy domain of Carthus, ceaselessly wartorn,[36] filled with mighty and vicious swordsmen[37][38] while producing an History of Lothric

entirely unique branch of pyromancy,[39][40] until a brutal warlord known as Wolnir came along to defeat each of the region's warlords and claim their crowns to become the first High Lord,[41] whom his warriors served religiously[42] as he put countless civilians to death in an attempt to prolong his own life and increase his glory.[43] Eventually, Wolnir foolishly attempted to conquer the Abyss and was instead consumed by it, leaving him stranded in the Dark with only three bangles stripped from dead clerics keeping him alive as he lay there in fear.[44] There was also the matter of Lost Izalith, source of all demons, in the eons following the Witch of Izalith and her daughters, who birthed all pyromancy[45] and taught it to man,[46] being consumed by the Chaos Flame that they created[47] - only Quelana and the Fair Lady survived, and after teaching her spells to the Chosen Undead,[48] Quelana returned to Lost Izalith and stayed with her sister until they both perished.[49] During and after this time, the demons that spawned from the Chaos Flame came to form a culture within the ruins, learning to bury their dead and even crowning a king and prince; however, their antagonism toward mankind led Prince Lorian of Lothric to slay The Demon Prince,[50] who held the remnants of the Chaos Flame that spawned the demons[51] and whose defeat thus marked the beginning of the end for their race, which began dying out with no way of replenishing their numbers[52] and forced them into a paradoxical existence.[53] Eventually, only the Old Demon King was left guarding the ruins.[54] Note: the above information was subject to a slight, but notable retcon with the release of The Ringed City DLC, where The Demon Prince is fought - his boss Soul received a very rare rewording which changed the information presented, altering it from a confirmation that the Prince harboring the Chaos Flame upon his defeat led to the extinction of demonkind to a revelation that the Chaos Flame is instead shared between all demons, allowing The Demon Prince to be reborn from any one of them, as demonstrated during the boss battle.

Finally, there was what would become the Profaned Capital. Once subjugated by a Giant conqueror, the people of the land sought the mighty Yhorm, his descendant, to become their leader and protector,[55] which he did with benevolence toward his subjects and unrelenting force toward his enemies by fighting as a one-man army, though he became more reckless and aggressive after losing someone he wished to protect.[56] Additionally, to quell fears about the possibility of him turning on the humans, Yhorm gifted them the Storm Ruler, a weapon capable of killing him in the hand of a capable warrior. Befriending the boisterous Siegward of Catarina, [57] Yhorm gave him a Storm Ruler as well in the event that he would need to be put down one day, [58] and when the Profaned Flame of the realm began flaring up due to the curse of a certain clan of women,[59] Yhorm chose to become a Lord of Cinder in order to quell it despite the sneering of those who believed he was unworthy.[30] However, when he did so, the Profaned Flame erupted and incinerated Yhorm's subjects, reducing the Profaned Capital to a near-lifeless wasteland,[60] and would later be found by an individual who would use it to enact a terrible plot and coup: Pontiff Sulyvahn.[61] Born a Corvian inside the Painted World of Ariandel, but seeing no need to stay there since he had never experienced loss,[62] Sulyvahn ventured outside into the real world and, upon discovering the Profaned Flame, gained a powerful ambition to overthrow the old gods of Lordran.[61] To this end, he joined the governing body of Irithyll of the Boreal Valley and slowly amassed power,[63] first corrupting its Fire Witches with the Profaned Flame[64] and recruiting the knights to serve as his spies and executioners[65] before getting rid of his political rivals by giving them vile rings[66] [67] that twisted their minds and bodies, reducing them to savage and mindless beasts whom he sent off on indefinite missions[68] - most notably, he used this method to get the Dancer of the Boreal Valley, the daughter of Gwynevere who could contest his rule,[69] and her bodyguard Vordt out of the city, reduced to insanity[70] with no hope of return.[71] After setting up a barrier to prevent outsiders from entering the city[72] and recruiting surviving noblemen from the Profaned Capital to torture dissidents in the city dungeon,[73]Sulyvahn enacted the master-stroke of his plan by destroying the Blades of the Darkmoon and poisoning Gwyndolin,[74] whom he left in the gutted husk of Anor Londo to be consumed by another Lord of Cinder; Aldrich, Devourer of Gods.[75]

Aldrich began life as a cleric of the Way of White, but developed cannibalistic tendencies and began sadistically devouring men, whose screams of agony he reveled in,[76] to such an extent that his body swelled and bloated like a carcass before turning into sentient sludge, after which he was confined in the Cathedral of the Deep prior to being made a Lord of Cinder for his newfound might.[18] At some point during the final fading of the First Flame, Aldrich received a vision of an age of the Deep, which (combined with his lack of satisfaction over being crowned a Lord of Cinder)[30] led him to decide to devour the remaining gods in order to empower himself enough to bring about this age.[77] First, Aldrich corrupted the Way of White, who had been watching over his tomb,[78] and had more victims brought to him on the Road of Sacrifices running outside the Cathedral[79] from the Undead Settlement, warped by the preaching of the Evangelists,[80] before returning to his true home, Irithyll,[81] where Sulyvahn allied with him, fed him even more innocents (including children like Anri[81] and Horace),[82] and established the Aldrich Faithful to guard his new habitat, the ruined cathedral of Anor Londo.[83] Inside, Dragonslayer Ornstein had long since left in search of the Nameless King,[84] and the Silver Knights were twisted to serve Sulyvahn instead of the gods, [85] but Executioner Smough remained, steadfastly loyal to Gwyndolin in the centuries since his deposition of the cruel Lloyd[86][87] for the title of Allfather,[88] and fought valiantly as the last line of defense against Aldrich.[89] Ultimately, however, Smough fell and Aldrich devoured Gwyndolin, not only taking his body to use in combat, but accessing his memories of Crossbreed Priscilla and her Lifehunt Scythe as well.[90]

Note: Sulyvahn's relationship with Aldrich, and thus the extent of his evil, are dramatically different in the original Japanese version of the game. There, it's still confirmed that Sulyvahn came to power by overthrowing the old gods of Anor Londo, but Aldrich showed up without warning and battled him for dominance, resulting in Sulyvahn losing (which is why his attire is already damaged when you battle him) and giving Gwyndolin to Aldrich as appeasement. There is consequently no mention made of Sulyvahn feeding children, or anyone else for that matter, to Aldrich, and the two have no beneficiary relationship beyond a truce. Then there was the matter of Lothric, both the kingdom and the erstwhile ruler; King Oceiros and his queen strove to create an heir that could Link the Fire, resorting to unspeakable means[30] until Prince Lothric was born, albeit as a sickly, crippled child who was never given anything more than his swaddling clothes to wear[91] and fell far short of the champion his parents expected him to be.[92] Despite this, Lothric's mighty and noble elder brother Lorian elected to bear the weight of his curse, improving Lothric's health enough to make him a proper Lord of Cinder at the cost of crippling and muting himself[93] while inextricably linking their souls.[94] Additionally, the first scholar of the Grand Archives held doubts about the process of Linking the Fire and privately mentored Lothric himself,[95] which, combined with the emotional trauma of being raised as a sacrifice, left Lothric completely disillusioned with maintaining the age of Fire, such that when the First Flame began to fade, he and his brother simply retreated to the highest area of the castle, beyond the sealed-off Grand Archives,[96] and settled in to watch the Dark come.[97]

Note: the identity of the scholar who influenced Prince Lothric has one of two possible and important identities - he was either Aldia, the most notable scholar of the entire trilogy who sought a way to break the cycle of Fire and Dark by going beyond humanity's limitations, or Sulyvahn, whose Profaned Greatsword is visible on a statue of Lothric and who has ample reason to bring about an age of the Deep. As for the kingdom itself, it was founded on the Three Pillars, high-ranking personnel that ministered in different districts and professions: the scholar, who oversaw the Grand Archives and its vast store of knowledge;[98] the priestess, who led the church and the last of whom served as Prince Lothric's wet nurse;[99] and the knight, representing the standing army of the region[100] who were strong enough to both battle[101] and rear their own dragons and wyverns.[102] There was, however, a fourth and hidden branch of the royal authority - the hunters, who acted as the king's assassins and carried out deniable punishments that could not be publicly declared.[103] Unfortunately, the kingdom underwent several upheavals prior to the Ashen One's arrival; at some point, the converging nature of the land brought several other kingdoms from across the world to

inhabit the surrounding area, and this included a massive wall that cut off Lothric from the Undead Settlement beneath it.[104] During or after this, the holy maiden of the queen, Gertrude, was visited by a seemingly angelic being that blinded and muted her in the process of relaying a new and unique miracle to her -despite this, Gertrude succeeded in recording the tale, which became the foundation of an entirely new religion.[105] With the Three Pillars declaring this faith to be heretical, a massive civil war was waged between the Lothric Knights and those who pledged to follow Gertrude, now known as Winged Knights, which left the military in shambles.[106] Finally, King Oceiros, driven mad by the process of producing Prince Lothric, was led to the Grand Archives and joined a cult worshipping Seath the Scaleless,[107] resulting in him following the research of Big Hat Logan[108] and mutating into a draconic form that protected him from many assassination attempts,[109] though he never discovered the moonlight that he sought[110] and slipped further into madness over the uncertain fate of his son, Ocelotte.[111] Meanwhile, his queen (possibly Gwynevere), who had always cared for the nameless Undead,[112] going so far as to leave the prized Ashen Estus Ring in the Cemetery of Ash so an Unkindled could use it one day,[113] simply disappeared at some point after Ocelotte's birth.[114] The world faced its darkest hour yet when the First Flame began to fade for the last time; Irina of Carim, who had managed to become a Fire Keeper, foresaw a future of Dark[115] and, intentionally or otherwise, enacted a grand treachery that led to the First Flame completing going out, plunging the world into overwhelming darkness.[116] Following this, Champion Gundyr, already fated to eternal service,[117] arrived at the unlit Firelink Shrine and found that the bell heralding the fading of the First Flame would no longer toll[118] before the Ashen One traveled through space and time to reach the Untended Graves and defeated him, leaving Gundyr to become a sheath for the Coiled Sword,[119] meant for the Ashen One to pick up at the start of their journey.[120] Desperate to give the First Flame another chance, Ludleth of Courland willed himself into becoming a Lord of Cinder and broke time itself, sealing away the timeline that led to the age of Dark in the Untended Graves and rewinding to before the Fire was snuffed out, then crawled to the Firelink Shrine and took his place as one of the five Lords of Cinder needed to Link the Fire.

At last, the bell tolled, and the Ashen One awoke.[121] Some time prior to this, the Painted World of Ariamis had been painted over at least once, becoming the Painted World of Ariandel.[122] Within, the Corvians descended from the Crow Demons lived in peace - eventually, though, the painting made with blood began to rot, with the Corvians accepting the fate of burning the painting in order for a new world to be born from its ashes.[123] However, Friede, the eldest of the three sisters who founded Londor[34] and who had run away from it for reasons unknown,[124] entered the painting and, seeking to protect the Corvians from being burned,[125] manipulated Father Ariandel,[123] the painting's restorer, into flagellating himself over the Lordvessel containing the painting's Fire,[126] keeping it suppressed and allowing the rot to advance throughout the painting.[127] Aiding her in this endeavor were Sir Vilhelm, Friede's knight and hangman,[128] who followed her despite being formally dismissed from her service[129] and guarded the way to the Painting Woman[130] who could create a new world from the ashes of Ariandel,[131] as well as some Corvians who turned against their brethren and slaughtered those who would attempt to kindle the Fire.[132] In the present day, Slave Knight Gael enacted a prophecy indicating that the Fire of Ariandel would be set alight by two Ashes entering the painting[133] by recruiting the Ashen One to bring the flame to the frozen land, which he teleported them to.[134] Meanwhile, the Ringed City faced its own end; the castles and townships established around the world and across history piled up in a massive mound of stone and ash around it, coming to be known as the Dreg Heap, as the age of Fire came to a close, leaving only a scant few survivors like the Handmaid[135] and Unbreakable Patches, now calling himself Lapp after beginning to Hollow at long last.[15] Despite this, the city itself remained intact, due to Filianore's continued slumber maintaining the spell that preserved it against the flow of time,[136] though the egg tied to this magic was beginning to crumble;[137] to safeguard both the city and her, the Pygmies not only set up the Spears of the Church[138] under Judicator Argo to guard the chapel she slept in, claiming

that it was a defense against the Abyss,[139] but recruited Darkeater Midir, a descendant of the Archdragons who had spent his life battling the Abyss by the decree of the gods,[140] to defend her tower, though he would become afflicted by the Abyss itself and came close to turning on the Ringed City altogether.[141] Once again, the Ashen One would be led here by Gael, but this time for a far grander purpose - as one of the oldest beings in existence who fought underneath the gods[142] in the war against the Archdragons and many others afterward as an overlooked slave,[143] Gael sought to deliver a pigment made with the Dark Soul to the Painting Woman, his charge, so that she could paint a world outside the cycle of Fire and Dark that would never rot.[131] To this end, Gael had the Ashen One wake Filianore, pulling the Ringed City out of stasis[137] and allowing him to hunt down the Pygmies for their blood over the course of the ensuing centuries, fighting a near-endless battle that left his equipment almost destroyed from sheer overuse.[144][145] However, Gael discovered that the advanced age of the Pygmies had completely dried out their blood, rendering it unusable as pigment...so he consumed them one by one to take the Dark Soul into himself,[146] knowing full well that doing so would destroy his sense of self and leave him unable to return to the Painting Woman.[147] After devouring the last Pygmy, Gael battled the Ashen One, ostensibly for their portion of the Dark Soul, but when sufficiently injured, he saw his own blood contained the Dark Soul and realized he had succeeded, causing him to Hollow and let the Dark Soul take control of his body; [148] because of this, when the Ashen One finally slew him, they were able to collect the Blood of the Dark Soul and bring it to the Painting Woman for use in the new painting, only for her to reveal that she had intended it for Gael all along.[131] And at the Kiln of the First Flame, the Soul of Cinder, an empty husk of armor animated by the souls of everyone who had Linked the Fire,[149] awaited the Ashen One as the final defender of the First Flame...[150]

After the opening cutscene, you'll be dropped into the character creation screen - customize your Unkindled however you'd like, but make sure to pick the Knight class and Life Ring Burial Gift (notably, you will default to "None" for the latter, so don't forget to select it!), both for it being the most useful of the options and to start your ring collection with (1/107). When you're ready, hit "Finalize Creation" and rise and shine from your coffin in the Cemetery of Ash, the tutorial area of the game. The red messages on the ground (read with ) will explain the basic gameplay mechanics of attacking, locking-on, and so forth, so be sure to read them. Note: the game won't tell you this, but you start off with 7 gestures already learned. To properly track your progress toward the related trophy, these will be listed off now, and the gestures you pick up across the game will start numbering at 8: "Point forward" (1/33) "Point up" (2/33) "Point down" (3/33) "Wave" (4/33) "Jump for joy" (5/33) "Joy" (6/33) "Bow" (7/33 You'll discover your first enemy, a common Hollow, ahead - make sure to two-hand your starting Long Sword with , and you can take him out in a single R1 attack. The valley to the right leads to a Soul of a Deserted Corpse, the first of many Soul Chunks you'll be finding in this game -pocket it for now, and the guide will let you know when to use it later. Return to the intersection, kill the Hollow sitting in front of the altar, and collect the Ashen Estus Flask (restores FP gauge, or magic, instead of HP). From here, you'll see a Hollow up the stairs to the right that's staring at the wall and not you; because he hasn't noticed you, he's a prime target for a vicious backstab (performed by walking up slowly and pressing R1 when you're right behind him), which will do almost 3x the normal damage of such an attack - more than enough to kill him - and knock him flat in the process. A truly potent part of your arsenal.

However, you'll quickly find yourself being shot at by a Hollow with a crossbow in front of the exit leading to the fog ahead, so double back to the left side of the area and take out the Hollow waiting there, then head down the stairs to the "front" of the area to dispatch the one with the crossbow. From here, turn right and deal with the two Hollows that'll rush toward you...then prepare to deal with your first genuinely difficult enemy. The clearing beyond the water-filled path here contains a Soul of an Unknown Traveler (on the left side) AND a Ravenous Crystal Lizard, the grown-up version of the cute little Crystal Lizards you've been slaughtering in the previous two games; this thing hits like a freight train and moves just as fast, and while it DOES drop a nice reward, it'll take you quite a lot of effort to kill it now when you can instead come back later at a much higher level to take it on properly, so you're advised to just grab the Soul Chunk and get out of there. Now, from the main area, head to the exit and up a winding path to the left to reach and light your first Bonfire (Cemetery of Ash)... ...as well as receive your first new gesture, "Rest" (8/33). Next, head down the path beyond the Bonfire, kill the three Hollows down here, and turn right at the bottom to take a semi-hidden path along the edge of the cliff toward two more Hollows (one bearing a shield that'll drastically reduce the damage you do to him...unless you hold L2 before pressing R1 to use your Long Sword's Skill of guard-breaking and push it aside, allowing you to finish him off with ease. Behind them is a corpse holding 5 Firebombs, and once you've got those, return to the main path (resting at the Bonfire and re-killing the Hollows if you took a lot of damage in the process, as the author did) and run off the far edge overlooking a coffin to reach a corpse holding a Titanite Shard. This also gives you your first opportunity to perform a drop attack on the Hollow below the ledge to the right of here, and after taking out the crossbow-wielding Hollow in front of the arch, walk forward to face your first boss: Iudex Gundyr.

Uniquely, this guy won't do anything until you walk up and pull out the Coiled Sword lodged in his chest - but as soon as you do, it's go time. Certifiably the most advanced and challenging first boss in Soulsborne up until this point, Iudex Gundyr more than earns his keep as a gate to the rest of the game by putting your proficiency with rolls, attack timing, and stamina-preservation to the test; he has a long reach with his halberd and his attacks come out fairly fast, and he can turn pretty darn well despite his size during combos, so simply strafing around him won't automatically keep you safe. That said, his attacks are telegraphed heavily, so it's a matter of rolling as needed until he finishes a combo, then moving in to perform a couple of attacks before putting distance between the two of you and repeating. However, Iudex Gundyr will also be the first to display a trait shared by ALL bosses in this game that only a couple in the previous entries held: a second phase initiated once you deplete half of Iudex Gundyr his HP, where a canine monster will burst out of the roiling black matter on his shoulder and become a large extension of his range while also drastically changing his attack setup. Now, the ashen knight will be performing great leaps and slams while the monster will attack with wide-reaching sweeps and strikes - but contrary to what might seem sensible, it's now safer than before to stay close to Iudex Gundyr at all times, only rolling when he rises into the air to slam down again. Additionally, the monster is vulnerable to fire damage...and look at that, you just picked up some Firebombs to blast him with (ideally from a distance); if you're going to use these, make damn sure you lock onto him with R3 first. Overall, despite the challenge of facing a first boss like this with only your starting equipment and stats, Iudex Gundyr should prove a manageable challenge to you...but that doesn't mean you shouldn't put respect on his name.

Strategy Video Credit and thanks to Boss Fight Database for the video guide. With the former champion falling, you'll receive the Coiled Sword AND be Enkindled for the first time, boosting your HP by 30%! This is the equivalent of regaining Humanity in Dark Souls I & II, as it also allows you to interact with other players as invading/cooperative phantoms, but with the added HP bonus (and a cool visual flair) that makes it even more worthwhile to use when needed - it also fully restores your HP, so it functions as the only other healing item besides your Estus Flask (albeit only usable when not already Enkindled). With that done, open the doors at the end of the arena and collect a Broken Straight Sword from the corpse leaning against the grave. Beyond this, a path on the left side of the slope with two more Hollows leads to a corpse bearing a Homeward Bone (returns you to the last Bonfire you rested at while preserving your Souls), then head up the slope, killing the Hollows as you go. Just before the shrine, a path leading to the right will take you to a Starved Hound guarding a corpse with an Ember (a.k.a. the item that manually makes you Enkindled). Now, return to the top of the path and enter what will become your main hub for the duration of the game - Firelink Shrine.

This place ain't much compared to Majula, but you'll become attached nonetheless. First and foremost, walk down the stairs to the right to talk to everyone's favorite recurring character/concept, the crestfallen Hawkwood the Deserter.
